title: It Will Not Be Hurried
logline: In a small inland mill among the paddy of a southern district, every lot of rough paddy that comes through the gate is put through the same four unhurried operations — held under warm water for most of a day, driven through with steam, dried slowly on an open yard and then left alone in a bin to settle before it is allowed anywhere near the hulling stones — and the only way to ruin it is to shorten any one of them.
human_question: What is actually doing the work when something comes out right: the force applied to it, or the time it was given in the correct order?

place.what_kind_of_place: Low inland paddy country a dozen kilometres behind a southern coast, where the land runs in long shallow valleys of wet field with coconut and home garden on the rises between them, and small towns sit at the road junctions. The mill is not a factory. It is a yard, a shed and a chimney: a concrete apron the size of a tennis court for drying, swept and re-swept; a row of steel or concrete soaking tanks, open at the top, with paddy standing under warm water; a small wood-fired boiler with a stack of offcuts and husk beside it and a pipe run to a steaming vessel; a bank of holding bins; a huller, a polisher and a grader in a dim room where the air is entirely dust; and jute or woven sacks stacked in a corner in two heights, one for what came in and one for what will go out. The instruments are a wooden rake, a flat shovel, a hand plunged into the tank, a grain-moisture meter or a thumbnail pressed into a grain, a sieve, and a clock that matters more than any of them. Husk goes back under the boiler; the bran goes out in a separate sack. Nothing in the chain is automated end to end; every transfer is somebody with a shovel and a barrow.
place.why_it_is_worth_watching: Because the place is a procedure made visible, and because the procedure's whole content is waiting in the right order. Wide and from height, the yard is graphic in the plainest way: a rectangle of paddy spread two grains deep and raked into parallel bands, drying to a different colour hour by hour, with wet paddy fields on three sides in another green entirely, steam standing off the vessel in the early cool and a thin thread of woodsmoke going up. Raked bands on a drying floor, seen from above against the fields that grew the grain, is the most beautiful thing here and it is also exactly the concept: a result that arrives because somebody applied the right method patiently, and for no other reason. Close, the film is small decisive checks: a hand in the tank; a grain split with a thumbnail to see how far the water has gone in; steam coming through the mass and the husks starting to open; the rake turning the bands the other way; a handful lifted and let fall to hear it; a meter pushed into a bin; and a sample run through the huller to see whether the grain comes out whole or shatters. Nothing dramatic ever happens. That is the subject.
place.what_moves_or_changes: One lot at a time, always in the same order, with every step timed by the material and not by anybody's preference. Rough paddy comes in dirty and dry and is weighed and tipped. It goes under warm water for most of a day, and what matters is not the temperature or the hour but that the water has reached the middle of the grain. Then steam, which is short and irreversible: the starch sets, the grain darkens, husks split, and nothing after this point can be undone. Then the yard, which is the longest part of the day and looks like nothing happening: spread thin, raked, turned, gathered at noon or left, watched against cloud, and taken up when a meter or a thumbnail says so and not before. Then the part that is hardest to film because it is pure absence: the paddy sits in a bin and is not touched, so that the moisture inside each grain can even itself out and the stresses set up by drying can relax. Only then the huller, and this is where the whole day is scored: grain that was rested comes out whole, grain that was hurried comes out as fragments, and the fragments are worth a fraction of the price. Across a year the mill follows two harvests and stands half idle between them; across a longer clock, mills like this are being replaced by larger ones with enclosed dryers, and the open yard is the first thing to go.
place.when_it_looks_best: Inside a harvest, a few weeks after reaping, when paddy is actually arriving and the yard is in use every day; and inside that, a dry, bright, low-humidity stretch, because the yard is open to the sky and one shower at the wrong hour puts a whole lot back. Within a day the film is nearly forced: the yard from height in the first hour when the bands throw their own shadows and steam stands off the vessel in cool air; the raking through the flat middle of the afternoon when there is no shadow at all and the work is at its least picturesque; the hulling room in the last hour when low sun comes through the dust in the air and the room becomes visible; and the bins after dark, when the only thing happening in the mill is the thing that cannot be seen.

two_layers.without_the_philosophy: A film about one lot of paddy and the four things that have to happen to it in the right order. A yard of raked bands from above, with wet fields on three sides; sacks weighed and tipped; grain standing under water in an open tank and a hand going in to feel it; a thumbnail splitting a grain; a wood fire and steam coming up through a mass of paddy; husks opening; a rake turning bands the other way through a shadowless afternoon; a handful lifted and dropped to hear how dry it is; a meter pushed into a bin; a bin standing untouched in the dark; and then a huller, and a palmful of whole grain beside a palmful of fragments. With nothing said over it, anyone who likes a process with a fixed order, or the sight of a hot yard being worked, or the question of why one sack is worth more than another that came off the same field, has a whole piece here.
two_layers.with_the_philosophy: The same lot becomes the tenth item on a list the tradition keeps, and the item the list is easiest to misread without. The sources give ten kinds of accomplishment, and they run from a person becoming many and walking through walls down to a craft, a medical treatment, a piece of learning, and, in their own words, ploughing and sowing. The word underneath all ten is not magic but the bringing about of what was intended. One of the ten is reserved for the fully freed alone and it is not a feat at all: it is being able to meet what disgusts without recoiling, what attracts without being pulled, or both with the same steadiness, and the sources say it is reached through goodwill and through reflection, not through going cold. A mill where nothing is forced and everything is timed carries the tenth kind honestly, and lets the voice say plainly that the sixth is not on this yard, cannot be filmed, and belongs to nobody here. The voice never says the grain is a person and never says the miller has attained anything.

sequence.on_screen: First light, high above the yard. A concrete apron with paddy spread two grains deep and raked into parallel bands, drying unevenly; wet paddy fields on three sides; a thread of woodsmoke; steam standing off a vessel in the cool. A figure crossing the yard with a rake.
sequence.voice: Everything that happens here happens to the same material, in the same four steps, in the same order. Nothing in the building can be made to go faster. The only thing anybody can do wrong is shorten one of them.

sequence.on_screen: Rough paddy weighed and tipped into an open tank. Warm water over it. Hours later, a hand goes in to the wrist; a single grain is taken out and split with a thumbnail to see how far the water has reached.
sequence.voice: The word this film is built on is usually translated as power, and the source defines it much more plainly than that: the producing of what was intended, the obtaining of what was intended, the success of the means, and the result that success of means gives [C090-P4:L24]. On that definition the water in this tank is doing something the sources are willing to call by the same name as flight.

sequence.on_screen: The boiler: offcuts and husk pushed in, the pipe warming. Steam driven up through the soaked mass; the surface lifting; husks starting to open; the colour going over from pale to amber. The vessel closed, and then opened onto steam.
sequence.voice: The other book, on how any of this is prepared, uses two craft pictures: a goldsmith softening gold and a potter kneading clay, because the material has to be made workable before anything can be made out of it at all [C089-P4:L118]. That is what this fifteen minutes is. The grain is being made into something that will not shatter later.

sequence.on_screen: The yard in flat mid-afternoon glare, no shadows anywhere. Bands raked and turned the other way, then again. A handful lifted and let fall, listened to. A meter pushed into the heap. Cloud watched. The same yard hours later, one shade paler.
sequence.voice: Here is the item the sources put last on their list of ten. Success conditioned by right application: getting what was wanted, in any particular field, by applying the correct method to it [C090-P4:L121–L127]. The source names what counts — a craft, a piece of music or arithmetic, medical work, the three Vedas, the whole canon, any learning at all, and then, in its own words, at the very least ploughing and sowing [C090-P4:L127].

sequence.on_screen: The bins after dark. Paddy standing still, nobody in the room, a single bulb. A hand resting on the outside of a bin. Then morning, and the same bin opened and a scoop taken out.
sequence.voice: This is the step that cannot be photographed. The grain is left alone so that the water inside each one can even itself out and the stresses put into it by drying can let go. The sources are blunt about the equivalent point: merely thinking a thing or saying it achieves nothing [C089-M:L25]. What produces a result is a method, repeated, in an order, including the parts of it where nothing is being done.

sequence.on_screen: The hulling room in low sun through hanging dust. A sample run through; a palmful of whole grain held next to a palmful of fragments from a lot that came in wet and was turned round fast. Neither palm is anybody's hand in particular.
sequence.voice: And this is where the day is scored, without argument and without anyone's opinion. Rested grain comes out whole. Hurried grain comes out in pieces and is worth a fraction. The sources are equally unsentimental about how rare their own accomplishments are, and say each rung of them is reached by one in a very great many [C089-P4:L98].

sequence.on_screen: A poor lot and a good lot going through exactly the same operations, intercut without comment: the same tank, the same steam, the same yard, the same bin, the same wait. Sacks stacked in two heights against a wall.
sequence.voice: One of the ten is reserved for the fully freed and it is not a feat. It is dwelling without revulsion among what is repulsive, or with revulsion toward what everyone else holds high, or evenly balanced toward both [C090-P4:L85–L87; C090-M:L13]; and the source says it is reached by spreading goodwill or by attention to the elements, not by going cold. That is an inner response. It cannot be filmed, it is not on this yard, and nobody in this building is being described as having it.

sequence.on_screen: Last light. The swept, empty yard from height, the fields around it going dark, the boiler damped down, sacks in a row. Nothing moving.
sequence.voice: Three more things this film is not saying. The sources' resolve comes only after a very long, rule-bound training on top of the deepest absorptions, never from wishing [C090-P:L25–L46]. These capacities are treated as worldly, as a support for the work of understanding rather than the point of it, and the books tell the practitioner not to be satisfied with them at all [C089-P4:L26; C089-P4:L730]. And nothing here is anybody's desert. A sack that is worth less came off a field with more rain on it. Nobody's good year is a verdict and nobody's bad one is either.

concept_merge.why_together: C090 supplies the list and its two ends; C089 supplies what readiness actually costs. C090 defines the word itself as the producing and obtaining of what was intended and as success of the means [C090-P4:L24], and its tenth kind is success conditioned by right application, which the source says is getting what is wanted in any particular field by applying the correct method, and which it fills out with crafts, arithmetic and music, medical work, the Vedas, the canon, learning of any kind, and at the very least ploughing and sowing [C090-P4:L121–L127; C090-P4:L127]. Its sixth kind is the one reserved for the fully freed and is not a feat at all: dwelling without revulsion among the repulsive, or with revulsion toward what others prize, or evenly toward both, reached by spreading goodwill or by attention to the elements [C090-P4:L85–L87; C090-M:L13]. C089 states what the sources think produces any of it: mere thinking or saying achieves nothing [C089-M:L25]; the mind has to be made workable first, which it illustrates with a goldsmith softening gold and a potter kneading clay [C089-P4:L118]; each rung is reached by one in a very great many [C089-P4:L98]; and the powers are worldly, a support for the development of wisdom rather than its point, with the practitioner told not to be satisfied with them [C089-P4:L26; C089-P4:L730]. A parboiling mill is the tenth kind in physical form, its central operation is literally making a material workable so that it will not break later, and one of its four steps consists entirely of leaving something alone, which is the honest version of the sources' insistence that wishing does nothing.
concept_merge.what_it_reveals: That the tradition's own list does not put its highest mark on control over the world, and that the ordinary end of the list is not a consolation prize but a real category with a testable outcome. Said flat, ten kinds of power is a taxonomy with nine spectacular items and one mundane one. Put on a yard where a lot of grain is either whole or in fragments depending on whether four steps were given their time, the mundane item becomes something with a verdict attached, and the reserved item can be named out loud as the thing that is not on screen. The film also protects itself by construction. This idea's previous version filmed a worker who handles, hour after hour, what most people turn away from, and asked that person how they got that way; it is dropped entirely, because it makes an identifiable person's composure into a spiritual exhibit, because it invites the viewer to admire somebody for doing work the film has implied is degrading, and because the digest is explicit both that this equanimity is not coldness and that it is not an ordinary human capacity. The concepts are unchanged. The subject is now a procedure, with nobody's character on display, and the beat that once belonged to a person's steadiness now belongs to two lots of grain going through identical operations.

concept_links.why: The film is the digest's list read from its ordinary end, with its reserved item named and left off screen. The definition of the word as producing and obtaining what was intended, and as success of the means, is spoken over paddy going under water [C090-P4:L24], which is the digest's own point that the word underneath all ten is accomplishment rather than magic. The tenth kind is spoken over the drying yard, with the source's own catalogue given in its own order and its own words, ending on ploughing and sowing [C090-P4:L121–L127; C090-P4:L127]. The sixth kind is stated once, late, over a poor lot and a good lot going through identical operations, and the same beat says in as many words that it is an inner response, that it cannot be filmed, that it is not on this yard and that nobody in the building is being described as having it [C090-P4:L85–L87; C090-M:L13]; the source's own means, spreading goodwill and attention to the elements, are named, because the digest is explicit that this equanimity is balance reached that way and not coldness or indifference to other people's suffering. Every limit in the digest is honoured and three of them are on screen. 'Manifest your intentions' is refused out loud in the closing beat, which states that the source's resolve comes only after long, rule-bound training on the deepest absorptions [C090-P:L25–L46]. 'Good people are protected' is impossible here: there are no protection stories in the film, no story of anybody unharmed, and the closing beat says that a sack worth less came off a field with more rain on it. Prosperity-as-virtue is refused in the same breath, and the merit stories of endless rice, gold rams and mountains of gold are not cited, narrated or alluded to. Charms and lore are not endorsed and not mocked; that kind is not in the film. The miraculous feats are not presented as fact and not debunked, because they are not narrated at all. And no real person's calm, skill or composure is presented as an attainment: the film has no interview, no named worker and no account of anybody's history, and the one beat that could have been about a person's steadiness is about two lots of grain instead.

Four of this concept's statements are narrated and each is placed on the only thing that can carry it. The goldsmith softening gold and the potter kneading clay, the source's own image for making the material workable before anything can be made of it, is spoken over the steaming, which is precisely the operation that stops the grain shattering later [C089-P4:L118]. The Margaya's flat statement that merely thinking or saying a thing achieves nothing is spoken over the one step that consists of leaving something entirely alone, which is where a viewer is most likely to assume nothing is happening [C089-M:L25]. The ladder of rarity, one in a very great many at each rung, is spoken over whole grain beside fragments [C089-P4:L98]. And the closing movement carries the digest's corrections: these are worldly benefits that steady a practitioner for the development of wisdom, and the practitioner is told not to be satisfied with them at all [C089-P4:L26; C089-P4:L730]. Every limit in the digest is honoured. 'Manifest your reality' is refused by construction and by name. Meditation is not sold as producing abilities. Mind-reading, past-life recall and the divine ear are not in the film in any form, so they cannot be recast as empathy, therapy or attentiveness. The miracle narratives are not presented as documentary fact. Above all, the digest's warning about the divine-eye material that links poverty, low birth and appearance to past deeds is treated as an absolute floor: none of that material is cited, narrated, paraphrased or implied anywhere, the film contains no verdict on anybody's circumstances, and the closing beat states plainly that a poor lot is not anybody's desert. The procedure for making amends by speech, the torch and axe similes and the sound-training sequence are not used.

what_the_viewer_could_understand: That the tradition's ten kinds of accomplishment run from the spectacular down to a craft, a treatment, a piece of learning and, in the source's own words, ploughing and sowing, and that the word underneath all of them means bringing about what was intended; that the kind reserved for the fully freed is not a feat but an even response to what disgusts and what attracts, reached through goodwill and reflection rather than through going cold; and that the sources hold that nothing of this comes from wishing, that the material has to be made workable first, and that the practitioner is told not to be satisfied with any of it. The mill is an analogy for the ordinary end of that list and the film says so; nobody in it is described as having attained anything, and nobody's circumstances are presented as deserved.
what_must_be_real: The mill's own lots, in its own order, at its own speed. No soak is shortened or lengthened, no steaming is repeated, no yard is raked for a second take, no bin is opened early, and no lot is hurried or held back for the light or the camera. If a lot is spoiled by rain, or comes out as fragments, the film has that lot and keeps it. Nothing about how the boiler, the steaming vessel or the hot yard is worked may be altered for a shot, and nobody is asked to stand near any of them for a frame they would not otherwise be standing in. Nobody is named, followed as a character, or interviewed about patience, steadiness or how they got used to the work; the one comparison in the film is between two lots of grain and not between two people. No grower's name, no price, no weighbridge slip and no account book is put on screen, and the mill's customers are not identified. The mill decides what is filmed under its own roof.
position_hint: late in the group, after the films about what the texts call powers have been set up, and before any closing film: it is the beat that turns the group's idea of power around, by reading the tradition's own list from its ordinary end, and it needs a viewer who has already heard the spectacular end of that list named. It should not sit next to another film built on a fixed procedure. No location reasoning is involved.
risks: Letting any worker's steadiness, endurance or skill become the thing being admired, which is the exact failure the previous version of this idea committed.
Implying that the mundane end of the list is a consolation prize, or on the other side that mastering a process is a spiritual attainment.
Letting a poor lot, or a grower who brought in wet paddy, read as somebody's fault or desert. Nothing in this film may look like a verdict on anyone's circumstances.
Any drift towards the sources' passages that tie poverty or appearance to past deeds. None of that material is in the film and nothing on screen may suggest it.
Prosperity reading as virtue: two heights of sacks against a wall must not become a moral chart.

Romanticising hot, dusty work. A wood boiler, a steam vessel and a hulling room full of grain dust are how people are actually burned and how lungs are actually damaged, and nothing about how they are handled may be arranged for a shot.
Aestheticising the drying yard until the film becomes a pattern piece with no argument in it.
Turning the mill's obsolescence into a lament, or into a verdict on the people still running it.
Letting the empty yard at last light stand in for the unconditioned, which cannot be filmed.
Putting the mill's prices, margins or customers on screen, which would turn the film into livelihood arithmetic and away from the concept.
drop_if: Parboiling with an open drying yard is no longer done at this scale in the district, so the four steps cannot be followed in one place.
No mill will let one lot be followed from the gate to the sacks on its own terms and at its own speed.
The filming window falls between harvests, so no paddy is arriving and the yard stands empty.
The mill cannot be filmed without the crew being in the way of the boiler, the steaming vessel or the hulling room for hours at a time.
The work can only be filmed by asking somebody to demonstrate or explain it, which would put a person back at the centre of the film.

connections.note: Two films in which a fixed procedure is the whole subject: one whose hours are set by a clock and kept whatever the conditions, and one whose intervals are set by the material and cannot be shortened at all.
Two films that keep a person's steadiness out of frame on purpose, and that state out loud that nothing on screen is anybody's attainment.

selection.reason: It reads the tradition's list of powers from the ordinary end, on a process whose whole content is time given in the right order, and it can name the reserved kind out loud while keeping it entirely off screen.

review.note: Rewritten into the footage-led shape on 2026-09-24, and the subject dropped entirely. The previous version filmed a worker who handles, hour after hour, what most people turn away from, without flinching, and asked that person on camera how they got that way. That is gone. It makes an identifiable person's composure into a spiritual exhibit; it invites the viewer to admire somebody for doing work the film itself has framed as degrading; and the digest for C090 is explicit both that this equanimity is balance reached through goodwill and reflection rather than coldness, and that these are not ordinary human capacities, so an ordinary person's steadiness cannot be offered as an echo of it without the audience hearing an attainment. The idea's earlier record also had it merged into another film; that is reversed and this record stands on its own again. The concepts are unchanged and both links were re-read from the digests. The subject is now a procedure: one lot of paddy through soaking, steaming, open-yard drying and an untouched rest before hulling, where the only way to spoil it is to shorten a step. The beat that used to be a person's composure is now two lots of grain going through identical operations, and the sixth kind of power is named once and stated to be off screen and nobody's. Every citation was checked line by line against C090's and C089's digest evidence, and none was carried over from the old text. The divine-eye material that ties poverty and appearance to past deeds is treated as an absolute floor: it is not cited, narrated or implied, and the closing beat says in plain words that a poorer sack came off a wetter field and that nobody's year is a verdict.

suggested_location.name: A small parboiling rice mill in the inland paddy country of the Matara District, in and around the Hakmana and Athuraliya divisions

also_known_as.name: sambā and nadu
also_known_as.meaning: two of the common milled classes of rice sold on the island; the class a lot becomes depends partly on the variety and partly on how it was parboiled and milled
also_known_as.used_by: Sinhala usage and the local trade

also_known_as.name: parboiling
also_known_as.meaning: soaking, steaming and drying rough paddy before hulling, so that the starch sets, some of the goodness in the bran is driven inwards, and the grain resists breaking in the mill

also_known_as.name: tempering
also_known_as.meaning: the rest given to dried paddy before hulling, in which the moisture inside each grain evens itself out and the stresses set up by drying relax; skipping it is what produces broken rice

suggested_location.region: Matara District, Southern Province: the inland paddy valleys a dozen or so kilometres behind the coast, where wet fields run between coconut rises and the mills stand at the road junctions
suggested_location.why_here: Because the film needs a procedure with a verdict at the end of it, in a place small enough that all four steps happen within sight of one another, and this inland country has both. The valleys behind this coast are worked paddy, so a mill here takes rough grain from fields that are in the same frame as the drying yard, which is the film's best shot and its clearest statement at the same time. A mill of this size still dries on an open apron rather than in an enclosed drier, which is what makes the longest and least eventful step visible at all, and it still moves grain by shovel and barrow, which keeps every transfer on camera. The district is thin on this slate and its inland half is thinner still. The subject is a business rather than a household, so there is a body that can consent and no private life to expose; there is no auction, no landing and no market floor in the film, and no money needs to appear in it. And the concept's ordinary end is named by the source in exactly this register: the same list that contains flight contains, in its own words, ploughing and sowing.
what_to_film: The drying yard from height in the first hour and the last, so the raked bands throw their own shadows and the wet fields around the mill read as a different green, and again at noon when the pattern flattens out.
Rough paddy arriving, weighed and tipped, with no name, price or slip legible.
The soaking tank over hours from one fixed position: grain under water, a hand going in, a single grain split with a thumbnail.
The boiler being fed with offcuts and husk, and steam driven up through the soaked mass until the husks start to open and the colour goes over.
The yard worked through the flat middle of the afternoon: spreading, raking, turning the bands the other way, and the same frame hours apart so that the colour change can be seen.
A handful lifted and let fall, listened to, and a moisture meter pushed into the heap.
The bins at night, untouched, with nobody in the room, held long enough to be uncomfortable, because this is the step that cannot be photographed.
The hulling room in low sun through hanging dust, and a palmful of whole grain held beside a palmful of fragments.
A poor lot and a good lot going through the same four operations, filmed identically so that the cut between them carries no comment.
Husk going back under the boiler and bran going out in its own sack, and the swept empty yard at the end of a day.
suggested_location.access: By road inland from the coast and then on to minor roads and lanes; the mill is private commercial property, so everything depends on the owner agreeing, and on being approached through the agrarian services office, a millers' association or somebody they already deal with rather than cold. A mill will have views about competitors, prices and food-safety inspection, and a crew needs to be clear in writing that no prices, customers, weights or growers' names will appear. The hazards are real and domestic: a wood-fired boiler, a steaming vessel, hot grain, a yard at forty degrees, hulling machinery with open belts, and a room so full of grain dust that it should not be filmed without masks. The crew has to be able to stay out of the way of all of that for a whole day. Flying over the mill and the surrounding fields needs the owner's agreement and the neighbours' tolerance whatever the general position is. The work follows the harvest and stops in rain.
suggested_location.best_time: Inside a harvest, a few weeks after reaping, when paddy is arriving daily; and within that, a dry, bright, low-humidity stretch, because the yard is open and one badly timed shower puts a lot back. A block of consecutive days rather than single visits, so that one lot can be followed from the gate to the sack: the yard and the arrival on the first day, the soak and the steaming on the second, the drying across the third, the rest overnight, and the hulling on the fourth. A second visit in the other harvest is worth planning for, since a spoiled lot is part of the subject and cannot be arranged.

suggested_location.research_note: Desk research only, and unverified on the ground. From the sources above: parboiling is done in three stages, soaking, steaming and drying, with soaking aimed at getting enough water into the grain for the starch to gelatinise, steaming done with saturated steam for a period measured in minutes, and drying done by spreading the paddy thinly and stirring it; after slow drying the paddy must be tempered, which reduces the stresses created by drying and lets moisture move from the centre of the grain to the surface, and the resulting rice is firmer and less prone to breaking in the mill. General trade material states that many mills on this island use a parboiling system of controlled soaking, steaming and drying before milling. The administrative geography is confirmed: the inland divisions named here lie in this district, and the coordinates given are the published position of one divisional secretariat in that inland country, which is a direction towards the country the film needs rather than a survey. Everything specific to a mill is an inference and is the first thing to check on the ground: that mills of this size in this district still parboil rather than mill raw paddy only; that drying is done on an open apron rather than in an enclosed mechanical drier, which the film's longest step depends on; that a whole lot can be followed from the gate to the sack across consecutive days; and that the soak, steam and rest times are as described here, which are taken from general milling sources and not from this district. No mill, owner, grower, lot or household has been identified or approached, and no permission has been sought from anyone. No photograph of a mill, a drying yard or any part of this work in this district was found on Wikimedia Commons; the one image is of paddy fields in the inland area.

unknowns: Whether mills of this size in this district still parboil, or whether parboiling has moved to larger mills in the dry-zone paddy districts.
Whether drying is done on an open yard here or in an enclosed mechanical drier, which decides whether the film's longest step can be seen at all.
Whether the soak, steam and rest times assumed here describe how it is actually done in this district.
Whether a mill will allow one lot to be followed from the gate to the sacks without any step being adjusted, and with no prices, weights or growers' names on screen.
Whether a spoiled or broken lot can be filmed and kept, since the film's verdict beat depends on having both outcomes.
Whether a crew can be present in the boiler and hulling areas safely for hours at a time, and what protection would be needed in the dust.
evidence_class_note: Editorial proposal. The location is proposed by Claude from desk research and is unverified. No scene or shot is decided here.
